<u>Set 1</u>**G1.** The Daily Challenge office has a machine that outputs the number  $2.75$  when operated. If it is operated  $12$  times, then what is the sum of all  $12$  of the machine outputs?**G2.** A car traveling at a constant velocity  $v$  takes  $30$  minutes to travel a distance of  $d$ . How long does it take, in minutes, for it travel  $10d$  with a constant velocity of  $2.5v$ ?**G3.**  Andy originally has  $3$  times as many jelly beans as Andrew. After Andrew steals 15 of Andy’s jelly beans, Andy now only has  $2$  times as many jelly beans as Andrew. Find the number of jelly beans Andy originally had.

<u>Set 2</u>**G4.** A coin is weighted so that it is  $3$  times more likely to come up as heads than tails. How many times more likely is it for the coin to come up heads twice consecutively than tails twice consecutively?**G5.** There are  $n$  students in an Areteem class. When 1 student is absent, the students can be evenly divided into groups of  $5$ . When  $8$  students are absent, the students can evenly be divided into groups of  $7$ . Find the minimum possible value of  $n$ .**G6.** Trapezoid  $ABCD$  has  $AB \parallel CD$  such that  $AB = 5$ ,  $BC = 4$  and  $DA = 2$ . If there exists a point  $M$  on  $CD$  such that  $AM = AD$  and  $BM = BC$ , find  $CD$ .


<u>Set 3</u>**G7.** Angeline has  $10$  coins (either pennies, nickels, or dimes) in her pocket. She has twice as many nickels as pennies. If she has  $62$  cents in total, then how many dimes does she have?**G8.** Equilateral triangle  $ABC$  has side length  $6$ . There exists point  $D$  on side  $BC$  such that the area of  $ABD$  is twice the area of  $ACD$ . There also exists point  $E$  on segment  $AD$  such that the area of  $ABE$  is twice the area of  $BDE$ . If  $k$  is the area of triangle  $ACE$ , then find  $k^2$ .**G9.** A number  $n$  can be represented in base  $ 6$  as  $\underline{aba}_6$  and base  $15$  as  $\underline{ba}_{15}$ , where  $a$  and  $b$  are not necessarily distinct digits. Find  $n$ .


PS. You should use hide for answers. Sets 4-6 have been posted [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h3131305p28367080) and 7-9 [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h3131308p28367095).Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution for G1</summary>The sum of the  $12$  machine outputs will be   $$ 12\cdot2.75=\boxed{33}. $$    $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G2</summary>It will take   $$ \frac{10d}{d} \cdot \frac{v}{2.5v} \cdot 30 = 10\cdot\frac{2}{5}\cdot30 = \boxed{120} $$   minutes.  $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G3</summary>Let the number of jelly beans that Andrew had originally be  $x.$  Then, Andy originally had  $3x$  jelly beans.

We are given that
\begin{align*}
3x-15=2(x+15) &\implies 3x-15=2(x+15) 
&\implies 3x-15=2x+30 
&\implies x=45 
&\implies 3x=3\cdot45=\boxed{135}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G4</summary>Note that the probability that the coin comes up heads is  $\tfrac{3}{4}$  and the probability that the coin comes up tails is  $\tfrac{1}{4}.$ It follows that the probability the coin comes up heads twice is   $$ (\tfrac{3}{4})^2=\tfrac{9}{16} $$   and the probability that the coin comes up tails twice is   $$ (\tfrac{1}{4})^2=\tfrac{1}{16}, $$   so the answer is   $$ \frac{\frac{9}{16}}{\frac{1}{16}} = \boxed{9}. $$    $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G5</summary>We have   $$ x \equiv 8 \pmod{7} \implies x \equiv 1 \pmod{7}, x\geq 8. $$  Combining this with the fact that   $$ x \equiv 1 \pmod{5} $$   yields   $$ x \equiv 1 \pmod{35}, x \geq 8. $$   Hence, the minimum possible value of  $n$  is   $$ \boxed{36}. $$    $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G6</summary>Let  $X$  be the foot of the perpendicular from  $A$  to  $\overline{CD}$  and  $Y$  be the foot of the perpendicular from  $B$  to  $\overline{CD}.$ Clearly,  $ABYX$  is a rectangle, so   $$ XY=5. $$  Also, since  $\triangle{DAM}$  and  $\triangle{MBC}$  are isosceles, it follows that
\begin{align*}
CD &= DM+MC 
&= 2XM+2MY 
&= 2XY 
&= 2\cdot5 
&= \boxed{10}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G7</summary>Let the number of pennies be  $x.$  

Then, there are  $2x$  nickels and  $10-3x$  dimes. It follows that
\begin{align*}
1\cdot x + 5\cdot(2x)+10\cdot(10-3x) = 62 &\implies x+10x+100-30x=62 
&\implies 19x=38 
&\implies x=2 
&\implies 10-3x=10-3\cdot2=10-6=\boxed{4}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G8</summary>We have
\begin{align*}
k &= [ACE] 
&= \frac{2}{3}\cdot [ACD] 
&= \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{3} \cdot [ABC] 
&= \frac{2}{9} \cdot 9\sqrt{3} 
&= 2\sqrt{3},
\end{align*}
so the answer is   $$ k^2=(2\sqrt{3})^2=\boxed{12}. $$    $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for G9</summary>We have
\begin{align*}
36a+6b+a=15b+a &\implies 36a=9b 
&\implies b=4a.
\end{align*}
Since  $1\leq a,b \leq 5,$  it follows that  $a=1, b=4.$  Hence,
\begin{align*}
n&= \underline{aba}_6 
&=\underline{141}_6 
&= 36+4\cdot6+1 
&= 36+24+1 
&= \boxed{61}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution for G21</summary>The probability that Nate flips the coin exactly  $12$  times is the probability that the desired sequence (head, head, tail) does not occur in the first  $9$  flips but it does occur in the last  $3$  flips.

In total, there are  $2^{12}=4096$  ways to flip a coin  $12$  times.

By the Principle of Inclusion Exclusion, the number of ways to flip the coin the first  $9$  times such that the desired sequence of flips doesn't occur is   $$ 2^9 - 7\cdot2^6+\binom{5}{2}2^3-1 = 512-448+80-1 = 143, $$   and their is exactly  $1$  way for the last three flips to be the desired sequence, so the probability is   $$ \frac{143}{4096}. $$   Hence, the answer is   $$ 143+4096=\boxed{4329}. $$    $\square$</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>2 cases, convex and non convex</summary>Let  $w =\angle (AB,CD)$  be the smallest of angles defined by lines  $AB$  and  $CD$  $\bullet$  1st case - convex

Let segment  $AB$  intersect segment  $CD$  at point  $O$ . 
Draw lines parallel to  $AB$  passing through points  $C,D$ .
Draw lines parallel to  $CD$  passing through points  $A,B$ .

Denote  $KLMN$  the parallelogram defined by the intersection of those pairs of parallel lines. $[ABCD]=\frac{[KLMN]}{2 }=\frac{2[KLN]}{2}= [KLN]=\frac12 \cdot  KL\cdot KN \cdot \sin \angle LKN=\frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD \cdot \sin w \le  \frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD$  and equality holds when  $ \sin w =1 \Leftrightarrow AB \perp CD$ So in convex case , max area is  $\frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD$  $\bullet$  2nd case - non convex

WLOG, let the line  $AB$  intersect the line  $CD$  but such that segment  $AB$  does not intersect the segment  $CD$ , and  $A$  be the longest point then  $B$  from line  $CD$ Let  $M,N$  be the projections of  $A,B$  on line  $CD$  respectively
let  $O$  be the projection of  $B$  on segment  $AM$  $[ABCD] =[BCD]- [ACD]= \frac12 \cdot (AM- BN)=\frac12 \cdot  CD \cdot  AO=\frac12 \cdot  CD \cdot  AB \cdot sin \angle OAB=\frac12\cdot  CD \cdot  AB \cdot  \ sin w  \le  \frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD$  and equality holds  when  $ \sin w =1 \Leftrightarrow AB \perp CD$ So again in non convex case , max area is   $\frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD$ At any case max is  $\frac12 \cdot AB \cdot CD= \frac12 \cdot 10 \cdot 7=35$</details>

**p1.** Find the last digit of  $2022^{2022}$ .**p2.** Let  $a_1 < a_2 <... < a_8$  be eight real numbers in an increasing arithmetic progression. If  $a_1 + a_3 + a_5 + a_7 = 39$  and  $a_2 + a_4 + a_6 + a_8 = 40$ , determine the value of  $a_1$ .**p3.** Patrick tries to evaluate the sum of the first  $2022$  positive integers, but accidentally omits one of the numbers,  $N$ , while adding all of them manually, and incorrectly arrives at a multiple of  $1000$ . If adds correctly otherwise, find the sum of all possible values of  $N$ .**p4.** A machine picks a real number uniformly at random from  $[0, 2022]$ . Andrew randomly chooses a real number from  $[2020, 2022]$ . The probability that Andrew’s number is less than the machine’s number is  $\frac{m}{n}$  where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find  $m + n$ .**p5.** Let  $ABCD$  be a square and  $P$  be a point inside it such that the distances from  $P$  to sides  $AB$  and  $AD$  respectively are  $2$  and  $4$ , while  $PC = 6$ . If the side length of the square can be expressed in the form  $a +\sqrt{b}$  for positive integers  $a, b$ , then determine  $a + b$ .**p6.** Positive integers  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{20}$  sum to  $57$ . Given that  $M$  is the minimum possible value of the quantity  $a_1!a_2!...a_{20}!$ , find the number of positive integer divisors of  $M$ .**p7.** Jessica has  $16$  balls in a box, where  $15$  of them are red and one is blue. Jessica draws balls out the box three at a time until one of the three is blue. If she ever draws three red marbles, she discards one of them and shuffles the remaining two back into the box. The expected number of draws it takes for Jessica to draw the blue ball can be written as a common fraction  $\frac{m}{n}$   where  $m, n$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find  $m + n$ .**p8.** The Lucas sequence is defined by these conditions:  $L_0 = 2$ ,  $L_1 = 1$ , and  $L_{n+2} =L_{n+1} +L_n$  for all  $n \ge 0$ . Determine the remainder when  $L^2_{2019} +L^2_{2020}$  is divided by  $L_{2023}$ .**p9.** Let  $ABCD$  be a parallelogram. Point  $P$  is selected in its interior such that the distance from  $P$  to  $BC$  is exactly  $6$  times the distance from  $P$  to  $AD$ , and  $\angle APB = \angle CPD = 90^o$ . Given that  $AP = 2$  and  $CP = 9$ , the area of  $ABCD$  can be expressed as  $m\sqrt{n}$  where  $m$  and  $n$  are positive integers and  $n$  is not divisible by the square of any prime. Find  $m + n$ .**p10.** Consider the polynomial  $P(x) = x^{35} + ... + x + 1$ . How many pairs  $(i, j)$  of integers are there with  $0 \le i < j \le 35$  such that if we flip the signs of the  $x^i$  and  $x^j$  terms in  $P(x)$  to form a new polynomial  $Q(x)$ , then there exists a nonconstant polynomial  $R(x)$  with integer coefficients dividing both  $P(x)$  and  $Q(x)$ ?


PS. You should use hide for answers.  Collected [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c5h2760506p24143309).
solution_md:
P9:
Alternative solution.
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Letting the feet of the perpendiculars from  $P$  to  $BC, AD$  be  $E, F$ , respectively and then starting in much the same way as soryn’s solution at #6 above, we get $BP = \frac{4}{3} DP$ .
Next,  $[ADP] + [CPB] = \frac{1}{2} (AD \cdot FP + BC \cdot PE)$  $= \frac{1}{2} AD (FP + PE)$  $= \frac{1}{2} \cdot AD \cdot FE$  $=\frac{1}{2} [ABCD]$ , 
since the area of a parallelogram is equal to the length of one side multiplied by the perpendicular distance to the opposite side. 
Therefore  $[APB] + [CPD] = \frac{1}{2} [ABCD]$ Now  $[ABCD] = 2 ([APB] + [CPB]$  $= 2(\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot PB + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9 \cdot DP)$  $= 2 PB + 9 DP$  $= \frac{8}{3} DP + \frac{27}{3} DP$  $=\frac{35 DP}{3}$ .
Next  $DP^{2} = DC^{2} - 81$  $DC^{2} = AB^{2} = 4 + PB^{2} = 4 + \frac{16}{9} DP^{2}$ .
Therefore  $DP^{2} + 81 = 4 + \frac{16}{9} DP^{2}$  $\frac{7 DP^{2}}{9} = 77$  $DP = 3 \sqrt{11}$ So, since  $[ABCD] = \frac{35 DP}{3}$ , $[ABCD] = 35 \sqrt{11}$  $= m \sqrt{n}$  where  $ m = 35, n = 11$ .
So  $m + n = 35 + 11 = 46$ .</details>

If  $AO$  bisects  $\angle IAC$ ,  $AB + AC = 21$ , and  $BC = 7$ , then the length of segment  $AI$  can be expressed as   $\frac{m}{n}$  where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution for p3</summary>Note that   $$ 6^{10} = (2\cdot3)^{10} = 2^{10}\cdot3^{10}. $$  It is not difficult to see that there are   $$ 11\cdot11=121 $$   total positive divisors and   $$ 11 $$   odd positive divisors, so the desired probability is   $$ \frac{11}{121} = \frac{1}{11}. $$  Hence, the answer is   $$ 1+11=\boxed{12}. $$    $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for p6</summary>There are two possible values of  $[ADBC],$  one of which occurs when  $C$  is in the interior of  $\triangle{ABD}$  and one of which occurs when  $C$  in the exterior of  $\triangle{ABD}.$  Clearly,  $[ADBC]$  will be minimized in the former case.

Let the foot of the altitude from  $D$  to  $\overline{AB}$  be  $X.$ By Pythagoras, we have   $$ DX=15, CX=6. $$  Hence, the answer is
\begin{align*}
[ADBC] &= [ABD] - [ABC] 
&= \frac{AB\cdot DX}{2} - \frac{AB\cdot CX}{2} 
&= \frac{AB}{2} \left(DX-CX\right) 
&= \frac{16}{2} \left(15-6\right) 
&= 8\cdot9 
&= \boxed{72}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>
<details><summary>Solution for p8</summary>Note that the maximum possible sum of three standard  $6$ -sided dice is  $18$  and the minimum possible sum of two standard  $6$ -sided dice is  $2.$ It follows that the two  $6$ -sided dice must have a sum of  $2$  and the other three must have a sum of  $16.$ It is easy to see that the two  $6$ -sided dice must both show a  $1$  and the other three dice can show  $5,5,6$  or  $6,6,4.$ There are   $$ \binom{5}{2}=10 $$   ways to choose the pair of  $6$ -sided dice,  $1$  way to choose which numbers are on those dice,  $2$  ways to choose whether the remaining dice are  $6,6,4$  or  $5,5,6,$  and in both of those ways, there are  $3$  ways to choose which dice show which numbers, so the total number of desired ways is   $$ 10\cdot1\cdot2\cdot3 = 60. $$   Therefore, the desired probability is   $$ \frac{60}{216} = \frac{5}{18}, $$   so the answer is   $$ 5+18=\boxed{23}. $$    $\square$</details>

Andy and Harry are trying to make an O for the MOAA logo. Andy starts with a circular piece of leather with radius 3 feet and cuts out a circle with radius 2 feet from the middle. Harry starts with a square piece of leather with side length 3 feet and cuts out a square with side length 2 feet from the middle. In square feet, what is the positive difference in area between Andy and Harry's final product to the nearest integer?

*Proposed by Andy Xu*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that the area of Andy's O is   $$ 9\pi - 4\pi = 5\pi, $$   and the area of Harry's O is   $$ 9-4=5, $$   so the difference between the areas is   $$ 5\pi - 5. $$  Using the approximation  $\pi = 3.14,$  this is
\begin{align*}
5\cdot3.14-5 &= 15.7 - 5 
&= 10.7 
&\approx \boxed{11}.
\end{align*} $\square$</details>

Let  $P(x)$  be a nonzero quadratic polynomial such that  $P(1) = P(2) = 0$ . Given that  $P(3)^2 = P(4)+P(5)$ , find  $P(6)$ .

*Proposed by Andy Xu*
solution_md: Interesting condition... <details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $p(x) = ax^2+bx+c$ , so  $a+b+c=0, 4a+2b+c = 0$ . This means that  $3a + b = 0$ , so  $b = -3a$  and  $c = 2a$ . Thus, we can write the polynomial as  $ax^2+(-3a)x+2a$ , and we have  $(2a)^2 = 16a-12a+2a+25a-15a+2a = 4a+10a+4a = 18a$ , so  $4a^2 = 18a$  or  $4a = 18$ , meaning that  $a = \frac{9}{2}$ . The polynomial is  $\frac{9}{2}x^2-\frac{27}{2}x+9$ , and we have  $\frac{9}{2} \cdot 36 - \frac{27}{2} \cdot 6 + 9 = \boxed{90}$ .</details>

stem_md: Let $\triangle{ABC}$ be a triangle with $AB = 10$ and $AC = 11$ . Let $I$ be the center of the inscribed circle of $\triangle{ABC}$ . If $M$ is the midpoint of $AI$ such that $BM = BC$ and $CM = 7$ , then $BC$ can be expressed in the form $\frac{\sqrt{a}-b}{c}$ where $a$ , $b$ , and $c$ are positive integers. Find $a+b+c$ . Note that this problem is null because a diagram is impossible. *Proposed by Andy Xu*
solution_md:
We have  $2(BM^2-MC^2)=BA^2-AC^2+BI^2-IC^2$ . This is equivalent to
\begin{align*}
2BC^2-98&=100-121+(s-11)^2-(s-10)^2
2BC^2-98&=-2s
2BC^2-98&=-BC-21
2BC^2+BC-77&=0
BC&=\frac{\sqrt{617}-1}4.
\end{align*}

Therefore,  $a=617$ ,  $b=1$ , and  $c=4$ , so  $a+b+c=\boxed{622}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $ABCD$  be a square with side length  $6$ . Let  $E$  be a point on the perimeter of  $ABCD$  such that the area of  $\triangle{AEB}$  is  $\frac{1}{6}$  the area of  $ABCD$ . Find the maximum possible value of  $CE^2$ .

*Proposed by Anthony Yang*
solution_md:
4 cases

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $a=AB$   $1/6 \cdot [ABCD] = a^2/6$  

<u>1st case</u>If point  $E$  lies on segment  $AB$ , there is no triangle  $ABE$ ,so it's area  $= 0$  contradiction

<u>2nd case</u>
If point  $E$  lies inside segment  $BC$ , let  $x=BC$   $[AEB]=1/2  \cdot  AB  \cdot BX= 1/2 \cdot  a\cdot  x=ax/2=a^2/6 => x=a/3$ In this case  $CE=BC-BE=a-a/3=2a/3$ <u>3rd case</u>If point  $E$  lies inside segment  $AD$ , let  $x=AE$ Similarly with 2nd case, we get that  $x=a/3$  and  $DE=2a/3$ Pythagorean in right  $ECD$ :  $CE^2=ED^2+CD^2=(2a/3)^2+ a^2=13a^2/9$  so  $CE =a\sqrt{13}/3 > a\sqrt9/3 =a$ <u>4th case</u>If point  $E$  lies on  $CD$  , then  $CE_{max}=CD=a<a\sqrt{13}/3 $  of 2nd case

In this case we could also have a contradiction as ie area of  $\vartriangle ABE$  is fixed and equal to  $a^2/2 =1/2[ABCD]\ne 1/6[ABCD]$ Finally, max wanted takes place in 3rd case and
  $CE_{max} = a\sqrt{13}/3  =2\sqrt{13}$  when  $E$  lies on segment  $AD$  at distance  $a/3=2$  from  $A$</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>result has been verified by official results</summary>Let  $AE=EC=4x \Rightarrow AP=3x, PE=x$  $[EBC] =\frac{[DBC]}{2}=\frac{[ABCD]}{4}$  $\vartriangle AFP \sim \vartriangle PDC \Rightarrow \frac{AP}{PC}=\frac{AF}{DC}=\frac{3x}{5x}=\frac{3}{5}=\frac{AF}{AB}$  since  $AB=DC$ Let  $AB=5y \Rightarrow AF=3y$  $\frac{[AFP]}{[ABE]}=\frac{AP \cdot AF }{AE \cdot AB}=\frac{3x \cdot 3y}{5x \cdot 4y}=\frac{9}{20}$  $\Rightarrow  [AFP]=\frac{11}{20} [ABE] \Rightarrow [FPEB]=\frac{11}{20} [ABE]=\frac{11}{20} \cdot \frac{[ABCD]}{4}=\frac{11[ABCD]}{80}$ So  $[FBCP]=[FBEP]+[BEC]=\frac{[ABCD]}{4} + \frac{11[ABCD]}{80}=\frac{20[ABCD]}{100} + \frac{11[ABCD]}{80}
=\frac{31[ABCD]}{80}=\frac{31\cdot 160}{80}=62$</details>
